newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia to propose lifting ban on extradition.
newsitem.headline: Colombia to propose lifting ban on extradition.

text.p: Legislation aimed at abolishing Colombia's constitutional ban on extradition will be ready to present to Congress later this month, Justice Minister Carlos Medellin said on Tuesday.
"There's no doubt about it," Medellin told reporters when asked if the legislation would be ready for introduction in Congress later this month.

Washington cited the Colombian government's failure to revive extradition -- banned under intense pressure from drug lords in 1991 -- among its reasons for last Friday's decision to "decertify" the country for a second year as a trustworthy ally in the war on drugs.

It also cited the government's failure to respond to last year's U.S. request for the extradition of four top cocaine merchants, including brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the chieftains of the Cali drug cartel.

Countries that are decertified face the threat of U.S. economic and commercial sanctions. The United States has fallen short of clamping sanctions on Colombia so far, but it could easily move to do so -- and even suspend banking services with Colombia -- if the government fails to bow to U.S. demands.

Medellin said the government's decision to seek to revive extradition, which was announced earlier this year, was a sovereign decision taken by the government of Colombia, however, "without pressure, without threats and without time limits which would, of course be unacceptable."

U.S. officials hinted, in announcing Colombia's decertification on Friday, that sanctions could be imposed on the country within six months if extradition had not been approved by Colombia's Congress.
But Colombian law stipulates that constitutional changes can only be approved by two separate sessions of Congress, so the ban on extradition is unlikely to be lifted before year-end.

Hundreds of Colombians, including three presidential candidates, a justice minister, high court judges, journalists and scores of police, were killed in a campaign of assassinations and bombings that drug lords waged against extradition in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Legislation that would have revived the practice was proposed by ruling party Sen. Luis Guillermo Giraldo last year. It failed to win much support, however, since it was presented without the central government's backing. It was also so watered down, after lengthy debates in the lower house and Senate, that it was eventually withdrawn.
